usage: I eat rice / I eat a meal
object marker 을; the all-purpose word for having any meal
subject marker 이 spotlights the rice itself
drops the particle in casual speech; works as a friendly greeting
밥하다 = make rice/a meal, not 만들다
examples: 저는 아침에 밥을 먹어요.
I eat rice in the morning.
simple daily routine with object 을
밥 다 먹었으면 같이 나가자.
If you're done eating, let's head out together.
casual 반말; 밥 here = the whole meal, particle dropped
식사 나오기 전에 밥부터 좀 주세요.
Before the meal comes, could you give us some rice first?
real restaurant line; 밥(rice) vs 식사(the meal) used side by side
nuance: 밥 literally is the bowl of cooked white rice, but by extension it is the default word for 'a meal' — which is why 밥 먹었어요? functions as a real greeting like 'how are you?', not a literal question about rice. Contrast it with 식사(食事), the polite Sino-Korean word for 'a meal': you offer an elder 식사하셨어요?, never the blunt 밥 먹었어요?. The verb is 먹다(eat), and to cook rice you say 밥을 하다 or 밥을 짓다, not 밥을 만들다. The big English-speaker pitfall is hearing 밥 only as 'rice' and missing that 밥 먹자 means 'let's grab a bite', and that to a boss you must upgrade to 식사 to stay polite.

usage: object marker 을; note 먹다, never 마시다 for a rice-side soup
subject marker 이 to warn about temperature
하고 = and; the two together are the base of a Korean meal
끓이다 = boil/cook soup, the set verb here
examples: 한국 사람은 밥에 국을 같이 먹어요.
Koreans eat soup together with rice.
simple cultural habit; 국 paired with 밥
국이 좀 식었는데 다시 데워 드릴까요?
The soup has cooled a bit — shall I reheat it for you?
everyday service line; 식다(cool down) vs 데우다(reheat)
찌개 말고 그냥 맑은 국으로 주세요.
Not a stew — just give me a plain clear soup, please.
real ordering line that draws the 국 vs 찌개 line
nuance: 국 is a light, broth-based soup with plenty of liquid that you spoon up alongside rice at nearly every meal. The near-synonym to separate it from is 찌개: a 찌개 (jjigae) is thicker, saltier, more concentrated and simmered right in a communal pot (된장찌개, 김치찌개), whereas 국 (미역국, 콩나물국) is milder and served in your own bowl. There is also 탕, a heartier long-boiled soup-stew (갈비탕). The set verb is 끓이다(boil/make), and Koreans 먹다(eat) soup with a spoon. The classic English-speaker mistake is reaching for 마시다(drink) because in English we 'drink' or 'have' soup — in Korean you 먹다 국, and calling a thick 찌개 a 국 will sound off to a native ear.

Saying 국을 만들어요 — the natural verb is 국을 끓여요 (to boil).

usage: subject marker 가 to describe the taste
please give a bit more kimchi
반찬 refills are free; 좀 softens the request
담그다 = ferment/pickle, the proper verb for kimchi
examples: 저는 김치를 정말 좋아해요.
I really like kimchi.
simple preference statement
이 김치가 잘 익어서 더 맛있어요.
This kimchi is well fermented, so it's even tastier.
everyday remark; 익다 = ripen/ferment, a key kimchi word
김치는 반찬이라서 리필이 돼요.
Kimchi is a side dish, so you can get refills.
real-situation note on the 반찬 (banchan) system
nuance: 김치 is salted, seasoned, lactic-acid-fermented vegetable — most often napa cabbage (배추김치) but also radish (깍두기), cucumber, and more — eaten as a 반찬(side dish), never as the main. The word to contrast is 반찬, the umbrella term for all the little shared side dishes: 김치 is one specific 반찬. The native-feeling verb is 담그다(to put up / ferment), and as it ages people say it 익다(ripens). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 김치 like a single countable food and giving it a main-course slot; another is using 만들다 — Koreans say 김치를 담그다. Note too that fresh, just-made kimchi (겉절이) and well-aged sour kimchi (묵은지) are different enough to have their own names.

usage: subject marker 가 to describe texture
-고 싶다 = want to; attaches to 먹다
굽다 (ㅂ-irregular) → 구워요; the verb for Korean BBQ
examples: 오늘 저녁에 고기 먹고 싶어요.
I want to eat meat tonight.
simple desire with -고 싶어요
고기가 좀 질긴데 더 익혀 주세요.
The meat is a bit tough — please cook it more.
everyday line; 질기다(tough) vs 부드럽다(tender)
우리 회식인데 소고기로 구울까, 돼지고기로 할까?
It's our team dinner — shall we grill beef, or go with pork?
real situation; 소고기 vs 돼지고기 specified for clarity
nuance: In everyday speech 고기 by default means red land meat — usually 돼지고기(pork) or 소고기(beef) — so 고기 먹으러 가자 implies a BBQ, not seafood. To be specific you compound the animal onto 고기: 닭고기(chicken), 소고기(beef), 돼지고기(pork). The words to contrast are 생선(fish as food) and 해산물(seafood), which Koreans do NOT file under 고기; chicken sits on the edge, so people usually say 닭고기 rather than bare 고기 for it. The set cooking verb is 굽다, a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 구워요/구웠어요 (not 'gubeoyo'). The English-speaker pitfall is the English umbrella sense of 'meat' that includes fish and poultry — in Korean, unmarked 고기 leans strongly toward pork/beef, and you should name the animal when you mean otherwise.

usage: subject marker 이; 싱싱하다 = fresh (of produce/fish)
topic marker 은 sets fish up as the contrasted topic
굽다 → 구워요; grilled fish is a classic side dish
examples: 저는 생선을 자주 먹어요.
I eat fish often.
simple eating habit
이 생선 진짜 싱싱한데 회로 드실래요?
This fish is really fresh — would you like it as sashimi?
everyday market/restaurant line; 회 = raw sliced fish
살아 있는 건 물고기, 접시에 오르면 생선이에요.
While it's alive it's 물고기; once it's on the plate it's 생선.
real-situation rule contrasting the two 'fish' words
nuance: 생선 is 生鮮 — 生 'live/raw' + 鮮 'fresh' — literally 'fresh(-caught) thing', i.e. fish as FOOD, on the market stall or the dinner table. The essential contrast is 물고기, the live fish swimming in water (a pet goldfish, fish in a pond): same creature, but 물고기 is the animal and 생선 is the ingredient. Sliced raw for eating it becomes 회(sashimi), and dried fish is 건어물. 싱싱하다/신선하다(fresh) is its habitual partner adjective, and you 굽다(grill) or 조리다(braise) it. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'fish' covers both the live animal and the food, so learners say 물고기 when ordering at a restaurant — ask for 생선 (or the specific dish) instead, and never call the fish you're about to eat 물고기.

usage: object marker 를; no plural -s needed
도 = also/too; 좀 softens the request
다듬다 = clean and trim produce before cooking
examples: 저는 야채를 많이 먹어요.
I eat a lot of vegetables.
simple healthy habit; mass noun, no plural ending
고기만 말고 야채도 같이 싸 드세요.
Don't just eat meat — wrap some vegetables with it too.
everyday BBQ line; 쌈 culture, 도 adds vegetables
메뉴에 채소 이름으로 적혀 있는데, 야채랑 같은 말이에요.
On the menu it's written as 채소, but that's the same word as 야채.
real-situation note on the 야채 vs 채소 register
nuance: 야채 means 'vegetables' as an uncountable mass — you never add a plural ending, even for a whole pile. Its near-twin is 채소(菜蔬): the two overlap almost completely, but 채소 is the more 'proper', Sino-Korean and slightly bookish term you'll see on menus, packaging, and nutrition labels, while 야채 is the everyday, conversational word (the 野 in 야채 is 'field', 菜 'vegetable'). For raw leaves you eat fresh, there's also 쌈채소/상추류. Habitual partners are 신선하다(fresh) and the prep verb 다듬다(trim). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: adding a plural like 'vegetables' (야채들 sounds wrong here), and over-using 야채 in formal writing where 채소 reads better. When unsure in writing, 채소 is the safe, neutral choice.

usage: object marker 을; mass noun, no plural
깎다 = peel with a knife, the set verb for apples/pears
박스/상자 counter; you count by container, not by 'fruits'
examples: 저는 과일을 매일 먹어요.
I eat fruit every day.
simple daily habit; 과일 stays singular
후식으로 과일 좀 깎아 줄까?
Shall I peel some fruit for dessert?
everyday home line; 깎다 + 후식 (dessert) collocation
선물용으로 과일 한 상자 포장해 주세요.
Please pack a box of fruit as a gift.
real-situation line; 과일 counted by 상자, gift culture
nuance: 과일 is the mass category 'fruit'; like English 'fruit' used generally, it takes no plural ending, and when you mean specific items you name them (사과 apple, 배 pear, 딸기 strawberry) and count with 개 or by container (한 상자). Note 과일 is native-Korean-feeling and general; the parallel formal/technical term you'll meet on labels is 과실(果實) or in compounds 과(果). Its signature partner verb is 깎다(to peel) — Koreans peel apples and pears for guests — and its taste adjectives are 달다(sweet) and 시다(sour). The English-speaker pitfall is forcing a plural (과일들 for 'fruits' is unnatural as a generic) and using 자르다(cut) where 깎다(peel) is expected; another is treating 과일 as a dessert by default — in Korea cut fruit is itself the classic 후식.

usage: 깎다 = peel; apples are peeled before serving
개 counts items; numbers use native Korean 두
examples: 저는 아침마다 사과를 먹어요.
I eat an apple every morning.
simple daily habit; -마다 = every
이 사과 좀 시지 않아요? 다른 거 주세요.
Isn't this apple a bit sour? Give me a different one.
everyday market line; 시다 = sour
사과 두 개 주세요. 빨간 걸로 골라 주세요.
Two apples, please. Pick the red ones for me.
natural market line; 빨갛다 = red, 고르다 = to pick
nuance: 사과 the fruit is 沙果/砂果 ('sand fruit'), while the homophone 사과 'apology' is a different hanja, 謝過 ('thank/decline' + 'fault') — identical sound and spelling, separated only by context. At a fruit stall or table it unambiguously means the apple; with verbs like 하다/받다/드리다 (사과를 하다 'to apologize') it means the apology. As fruit its partners are 깎다(peel), 빨갛다(red, ㅎ-irregular → 빨개요), and tastes 달다/시다. The English-speaker pitfall, beyond the apple/apology mix-up, is the color verb: 빨갛다 is irregular, so 'the apple is red' is 사과가 빨개요, not 빨갛아요. Counting also trips learners — it's 사과 한 개/두 개 with native numbers, not Sino-Korean 일·이.

usage: I buy it at the bakery
빵집 = 'bread house' = bakery; 에서 marks the place of the action
굽다 → 구워요; same verb as grilling/baking
examples: 저는 아침에 빵을 먹어요.
I eat bread in the morning.
simple breakfast habit
갓 구운 빵이라 아직 따뜻해요.
It's freshly baked bread, so it's still warm.
everyday bakery line; 갓 구운 = freshly baked
케이크도 빵집에서 파니까 빵 사러 갈 때 같이 보자.

real-situation note that 빵/빵집 covers cakes and pastries

The word itself isn't Sino-Korean; it came via Portuguese pão through Japanese, which is why it's written in the native-feeling single syllable 빵. The contrast to keep straight is 케이크(cake) and 과자(cookies/snacks/crackers): 과자 is dry, crunchy snack food, NOT 빵. Habitual partners: 굽다(bake), 부드럽다(soft, ㅂ-irregular → 부드러워요), 바삭하다(crispy crust). The English-speaker pitfall is narrowing 빵 to 'loaf bread' and so being surprised that a croissant or 단팥빵 (red-bean bun) is also 빵 — and that you 'eat' (먹다) bread, never 'drink' it even when it's soft.

usage: 마시다 = drink, the correct verb for any liquid
topic marker 는 marks milk as the contrasted topic
잔 counts glasses/cups of a drink
examples: 저는 매일 우유를 마셔요.
I drink milk every day.
simple daily habit; 마시다, not 먹다
우유가 상했는지 냄새가 좀 이상해요.
The milk smells a little off — it might have gone bad.
everyday line; 상하다 = go bad/spoil
커피에 넣게 우유 좀 데워 주시겠어요?
Could you warm up some milk to put in the coffee?
real-situation café request; 데우다 = warm up
nuance: 우유 is 牛乳 — 牛 'cow' + 乳 'milk' — so it specifically means cow's milk; for other kinds you compound, e.g. 두유(豆乳, soy milk) or 분유(粉乳, powdered/baby formula). As a liquid it strictly takes 마시다(drink), not 먹다 — though, importantly, casual Korean does allow 먹다 for consuming food/drink generally (밥을 먹다, 약을 먹다), so you will hear 우유 먹어 to a child; still, the clean textbook verb is 마시다. The near-contrast is 요구르트(yogurt) and 치즈(cheese), which are 유제품(dairy) but not 우유. Habitual partners: 차갑다/시원하다(cold), 데우다(warm up), 상하다(spoil). The English-speaker pitfall is defaulting to 먹다 from 'have milk', and forgetting the counter — milk is counted in 잔(glass) or 팩/병(carton/bottle), never with 개.

usage: 에서 marks the place where an action happens
에 marks the destination of movement
subject marker 이; 깔끔하다 = neat, clean
examples: 우리 이 식당에서 점심 먹어요.
Let's eat lunch at this restaurant.
simple line contrasting place-of-action 에서
저 식당에 가서 자리부터 잡을게요.
I'll go to that restaurant and grab a table first.
everyday line; movement 에 then 가서
회사 구내식당이 싸고 빨라서 점심은 거기서 해결해요.
The company cafeteria is cheap and fast, so I handle lunch there.
real-situation use; 구내식당 = staff cafeteria
nuance: 식당 is 食堂 — 食 'eat' + 堂 'hall' — an 'eating hall', i.e. an ordinary, everyday place to have a meal: a neighborhood eatery, a noodle shop, or a 구내식당(cafeteria). The register contrast is 레스토랑, the loanword reserved for fancier, often Western, sit-down dining; you'd call a humble 백반집 a 식당, never a 레스토랑, and a candlelit Italian place a 레스토랑, not a plain 식당. The crucial grammar point is particle choice: use 에서 for an action done there (식당에서 먹어요 'eat AT the restaurant') but 에 for it as a destination (식당에 가요 'go TO the restaurant'). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 에/에서 split, since English 'at/to' don't map one-to-one; another is reaching for 레스토랑 as the default word for any restaurant when 식당 is the everyday term.

usage: 보다 = look at; 봐요 in 요-form
메뉴판 = the physical menu card; 주세요 polite request
there are many menu items / choices
subject marker 가; here 메뉴 = the dishes available
메뉴 = a specific offered dish, not the list
examples: 메뉴 좀 보여 주세요.
Please show me the menu.
simple polite request at a restaurant
여기 제일 잘 나가는 메뉴가 뭐예요?
What's the most popular dish here?
everyday ordering line; 메뉴 = a dish, 잘 나가다 = sell well
메뉴 정하기 전에 메뉴판부터 다시 볼까요?
Before we decide on a dish, shall we look at the menu card again?
real-situation line using both senses: dish vs physical menu
nuance: 메뉴 (loanword from 'menu') carries two senses Koreans switch between freely: (1) the printed list of offerings, and (2) an individual dish/order — so 무슨 메뉴 먹을까? means 'which dish shall we get?', and 메뉴 정했어? means 'have you decided what to order?'. When you specifically mean the physical card you hand over, Koreans often say 메뉴판 (menu-board) to disambiguate. The dish sense overlaps with 음식(food in general) and 요리(a cooked dish), but 메뉴 frames it as a selectable option on offer. Common partners: 메뉴를 정하다/고르다(decide/choose a dish), 메뉴가 다양하다(varied), 오늘의 메뉴(today's special). The English-speaker pitfall is locking 메뉴 to the printed-list meaning only, then being confused by 이 집은 메뉴가 맛있어요 — which praises the dishes, not the paper.
